title: Parse-queue coalescing and lazy normalization to reduce prefill enqueue overhead
creator: Aisha Khan
description: Reduce CPU and scheduling overhead on the prefill side by coalescing short-lived parse jobs into larger normalization batches and deferring full unicode/normalization work until it is necessary (lazy normalization). Goal: lower per-request prefill overhead for short prompts common in prod while preserving correctness for infrequent complex inputs.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end correctness preserved for normalized outputs compared to baseline tokenizer for 99.99% of corpus (fuzz/coverage tests)
Median prefill CPU cycles per request reduced by >=15% on standard mix (short prompts <128 tokens)
Overall tail latency (95p) does not regress more than 5ms on the canonical load profile
Feature gated behind runtime flag and safe for canary rollout in Dedicated/Hosted
steps: Design coalescing queue module that groups parse requests by arrival window (configurable micro-window) and tenant affinity
Implement lazy normalizer: fast ASCII/utf8-plain path that skips expensive NFKC/NFKD unless heuristics detect nontrivial unicode sequences
Add collocated cache-key calculation so batches reuse a single KV cache lookup where possible
Wire feature flag and metrics hooks (per-batch size, miss/hit counts, deferred-normalize count)
Run unit + fuzz tests and throughput benchmarks, iterate on heuristics, then implement Rust hotpath for production service
benchmarks: Prototype (Go) on c5.large equivalent: median prefill latency -17%, CPU cycles/request -18% for short prompt mix
95th p latency saw +3ms in worst-case synthetic test when coalescing window set to 8ms; hedging disables coalescing for client-critical routes
End-to-end tokenization correctness matrix: 10M sampled tokens, 4 mismatches attributable to BOM edge-case which was fixed by fallback rule
risks: Coalescing can increase client-observed tail latency for latency-sensitive routes if window is misconfigured
Lazy normalization heuristics may miss rare unicode transforms leading to incorrect tokenization for some languages — mitigated with coverage fuzzing and an immediate fallback path
Shared KV lookup collocation requires careful key partitioning to avoid cross-tenant leakage — ensure strong tenant affinity and key-scope checks
